spoken: Around two hundred and forty BC, a scholar in Egypt worked out the size of the whole Earth.
Without ever going round it?
He didn't need to. He used a shadow, a distance and one idea from geometry.
And his answer was about 250,000 stadia.
That sounds precise. But even today, we can't say exactly how close he came.
So this is the story of Eratosthenes, and of a number we still argue about.
Eratosthenes was born around 276 BC in Cyrene, a Greek city in what's now Libya.
He studied in Athens for years. Then the king of Egypt, Ptolemy the Third, called him to Alexandria.
To run the Library of Alexandria, one of the largest libraries of the ancient world.
That's quite a job offer.
And the post also made him tutor to the future king.
He wrote about mathematics, geography, poetry, history and the stars.
His admirers called him Pentathlos, like an athlete who competes in five events.
And his critics called him Beta, meaning second best at everything.
Second best at everything is still quite something.
One thing he didn't have to prove was that the Earth is round.
They already knew that?
They had, for a century or so. Aristotle had pointed to the Earth's round shadow on the Moon during an eclipse.
And he noted that some stars seen in Egypt can't be seen from further north.
That only works if the ground curves between the two places.
Aristotle even reported a size for the Earth, which was four hundred thousand stadia.
Eratosthenes found a way to actually measure it.
Far up the Nile, on Egypt's southern frontier, lay the town of Syene. Today it's Aswan.
And Syene was known for something that happened there once a year.
At noon on the summer solstice, the longest day of the year, upright sticks there cast no shadow.
None at all?
None. Later writers also tell of a well there, where the noon sunlight reached all the way down to the water.
Because the Sun was standing straight overhead.
Syene was taken to lie on the Tropic of Cancer, the furthest north the Sun can ever be overhead.
But at Alexandria, on the coast, about 5,000 stadia further north, sticks still cast shadows at that noon.
And that difference is the whole clue.
If the Earth were flat, and the Sun far away, sticks in both places would cast the same shadow.
They don't. So the ground between them has to curve.
And how much it curves over that distance tells you the size of the whole Earth.
So he needs to measure how different the shadows are, and how far apart the cities are.
So how big was the shadow at Alexandria?
According to Cleomedes, it was read on a scaphe, which is a sundial shaped like a bowl.
A bowl, not just a stick in the ground?
A bowl. A pointer stands at the bottom, and its tip sits right at the centre of the bowl's curve.
So at noon, the tip's shadow falls on the inside of the bowl.
The arc from the foot of the pointer to the end of the shadow measures how far the Sun is from overhead.
That's neat. The bowl turns the shadow straight into a piece of a circle.
And at Alexandria, that arc was one fiftieth of a full circle.
In degrees, that's seven point two.
That's small. A stick would cast a noon shadow only about one eighth as long as itself.
And at Syene, at the same noon, the shadow was nothing at all.
Now comes the key idea. The Sun is so far away that its rays arrive almost parallel.
Let's draw the Earth, with Syene at the top and Alexandria a little way round.
At Syene, a ray comes straight down the stick. Extend that stick downwards, and it reaches the Earth's centre.
At Alexandria, extend the stick too. It also points to the centre.
And there, the ray meets the stick at seven point two degrees.
Now the Alexandria stick line crosses two parallel lines, which are the ray at Alexandria and the ray down the Syene stick.
That's the Z shape.
When a line crosses two parallel lines, the alternate angles are equal.
So the angle at the centre of the Earth, between the two cities, is also 7.2 degrees.
So the shadow in Alexandria is really measuring the curve of the Earth.
Syene and Alexandria are one fiftieth of the way round the Earth.
But is the Sun really far enough away for that?
Easily. Between those two cities, the rays differ by less than a thousandth of a degree.
Now he needed the distance between the two cities.
Cleomedes gives it as five thousand stadia.
And how was that measured?
Honestly, we don't really know.
Egypt did have bematists. These were professional pacers who measured land for farming and for taxes.
And some historians think his distance came from their surveys.
A Latin writer, some 650 years later, says royal surveyors measured it.
Six hundred and fifty years later. That's a long way from a first-hand account.
Either way, if five thousand stadia is one fiftieth of the way round, the whole way round is fifty times as far.
Fifty times 5,000 is 250,000 stadia.
From a shadow and a distance, he had the size of the whole Earth.
That's the story as it's usually told. But where does it actually come from?
Eratosthenes wrote it up in a book, On the Measure of the Earth. And the book is lost.
So we're relying on someone else's account.
Mostly on Cleomedes, who wrote a basic astronomy textbook.
And nobody knows when he wrote it, but it was somewhere between the first century BC and about AD 400.
That's a window of more than four centuries.
And Cleomedes says himself that his version is simplified.
His account talks about sundials, not a well. The well comes from other writers, like the geographer Strabo.
So the most famous detail isn't even in our main source.
And there's a second number.
The Roman writer Pliny the Elder gives Eratosthenes' result as two hundred and fifty-two thousand stadia.
Why the extra 2,000? Historians disagree.
Two hundred and fifty-two thousand divides evenly by every whole number from one to ten, but two hundred and fifty thousand doesn't.
And split into 360 degrees, it gives a neat 700 stadia for each one.
So some think he adjusted his figure, to make calculations easier.
Others think he defined a stadion of his own, from the size of the Earth, as Pliny's wording suggests.
That would make the unit itself part of the puzzle.
So how good was his answer? To check, we need his stadia in kilometres.
A stadion was 600 feet. But a foot wasn't the same everywhere in the Greek world.
Historians' estimates for the stadion run from about a hundred and fifty to two hundred and ten metres.
That's a spread of 40 percent.
And the real distance round the Earth, through the poles, is about 40,008 kilometres.
So here's what that range of stadia does to his two hundred and fifty thousand.
With a stadion of about 176 metres, he's about 10 percent too big.
With about a hundred and eighty-five metres, he's about fifteen percent too big.
But take Pliny's 252,000 and a short stadion, 155 to 160 metres, and he's within 2.4 percent.
So is the short stadion the right one?
One study found about 157.7 metres from ancient distances, but critics say it's full of errors.
So the famous claim that he was within two percent depends on choosing a short stadion.
That's a lot to hang on one unit.
But the method itself is sound. If you measure the angle and the distance accurately, it gives Earth's true size.
Cleomedes' version also rests on a few simplifications. Let's check them.
First, take the parallel rays. That one holds very well, as we've seen.
Second, it assumes that Syene sits exactly on the Tropic of Cancer.
In fact it's a little north of it, by less than a degree. Even there, the noon Sun wasn't quite overhead.
So no shadow was only nearly true.
And the tropic drifts, too. In Eratosthenes' time it lay about 0.3 degrees further north than today.
Third, it assumes that Syene lies due south of Alexandria, on the same meridian.
In fact it's about 3 degrees of longitude further east.
And the Earth isn't a perfect sphere, but slightly flattened, by about three tenths of a percent.
Still, the angle came out well. The two cities' latitudes really differ by about 7.1 degrees.
And he had seven point two. That's close.
What we can't check is the distance, because we don't know his stadion.
Measuring the Earth was only part of what he did.
In his Geographica, he mapped the known world on a grid of parallels and meridians.
It named more than 400 cities with their locations, and it gave us the word geography.
He also measured the tilt of the Earth's axis, and worked out dates in history back to the fall of Troy.
And his name lives on in mathematics, in the sieve of Eratosthenes.
The way of finding prime numbers?
Write out the numbers. Cross out the multiples of 2, then of 3, then of 5, then of 7.
And what's left are the prime numbers.
Though our earliest record of the sieve was written centuries later, and he may have named it rather than invented it.
Later writers used smaller figures for the Earth. Ptolemy's Geography used just a hundred and eighty thousand stadia.
And some seventeen centuries after Eratosthenes, Columbus read his work, but chose to believe in an Earth about a quarter smaller.
And a smaller Earth made the voyage west to Asia look shorter.
So let's put the whole idea in one picture.
There's no shadow at Syene, and a shadow of one fiftieth of a circle at Alexandria.
Parallel rays carry that angle to the centre of the Earth.
Fifty times five thousand stadia gives two hundred and fifty thousand stadia round.
How close was he? That depends on a unit we still can't pin down.
But the idea was right, and it measured the whole Earth from two cities in Egypt.
And it only took a stick, a bowl and a good argument.
That's not bad for a man his critics called Beta.
